doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Playing with Benny Goodman: eccentricities
summary: Stories of Goodman testing acoustics onstage and Jimmy Rowles' quip about his clarinet.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: What was it like to play behind Benny Goodman?

Great. What could I tell you. I mean he always played good. You’ve heard all the stories about the ray and all the unthinking, careless things that he would do, the thoughtless things that he would do. And he acted very strange on any number of occasions. One time he came out, we were playing the big music hall in Philadelphia, Symphony Hall I believe it’s called. Beautiful place. He comes out, the whole band is on stage, he walks out, uproarious applause, applause fades down, he’s holding his little clarinet like this © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

[whistles] almost like he’s testing the acoustics or something. And the whole audience, including the band is sitting there scratching their heads going okay. And this goes on for like a minute and a half, two minutes, right at the beginning of the show. And then finally he just said “Hello. Good evening. It’s so nice to be here. Where are we anyway?” But I viewed him as sort of a harmless sort of a talented idiot savant sort of. You know there’s a lot of artists like that. They’re brilliant artists, socially inept, just — they don’t have a concept that there’s even other people in the room, much less that they might be aware and might need to be communicated to, something basic like that. There’s a category of artists like that. And I love to witness and absorb and consume their works.
Yeah, and be part of it.

But you don’t really want to hang out with them you know? There’s some that way and he was one of them. I mean to give you an idea, we were playing in L.A. one time, and we were staying at the Ambassador, and Jimmy Rowles was playing I guess it was a solo gig. It may have been Dante’s, but I think it may have been somewhere else, I can’t recall. It was in the early ‘80s. And a bunch of us, including Scott Hamilton, Warren Vache and I think probably Cal Collins, Connie Kay, those were the kind of people that were in the band at that time, John Bunch, we went over to catch Jimmy. And we sat down and then he finished his set and he came over and he goes, “Hey, what are all you guys doing in town?” And we go, “Oh we’re here with Benny.” And his response is, “Does he still sleep with it?” Meaning his clarinet. Because the guy related to the world through his clarinet, although a lot of people will say he was as sly as a fox. Strange, with a purpose. But I don’t know if I buy that. I was up pretty close to it.
